title: Using FAR Proposal Debriefs to Improve Win Rates
summary: See how to request a government proposal debrief, ask the right questions, and apply the feedback to your next bid.
body_markdown:
A debrief is the one place where the government tells you directly what your proposal got wrong. FAR 15.506 requires agencies to walk you through your overall ratings, the major weaknesses or deficiencies evaluators found, and the award rationale, but that conversation only happens if you ask for it in time and know what questions to bring in.


**TLDR:**


- Submit your debrief request in writing within 3 days of receiving the award notice (or the exclusion notice, if you were cut from the competitive range); missing that window forfeits your entitlement under FAR 15.506.
- On DoD awards, required post-award debriefings add a written follow-up round under DFARS 215.506-70: 2 business days to submit questions, 5 business days for the agency's written answers.
- If you requested a required debriefing on time, GAO's 10-day protest clock runs from the date the debriefing is held, not from the award notice; confusing the two can cost you the protest.
- Structure debrief questions around Section M evaluation factors and log evaluator feedback against each factor to surface patterns across multiple pursuits.
- GovEagle's annotated outline maps each proposal section to the Section L, M and PWS requirements it must answer before drafting begins, so post-debrief gap analysis points to a specific section, not a general volume.


## What a Government Proposal Debrief Is


Under FAR 15.506, agencies are required to debrief offerors who request one, providing the basis for the[source selection decision](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/ssa-source-selection-authority) and contract award. Federal procurement under the Federal Acquisition Regulation is a structured, documented process: evaluators score proposals against defined criteria, and offerors have a right to understand how those scores were reached.


What you receive is specific to your proposal. The government will share your overall ratings, identify the major weaknesses or deficiencies the evaluation team documented, and summarize the award rationale. What you will not get is a line-by-line comparison to the winner's proposal or access to proprietary competitor information. Because the debrief arrives only after the decision is made, some teams pressure-test drafts earlier:[Chevo, a federal Mission Support Services contractor](https://www.goveagle.com/case-study/40-faster-proposal-prep-for-federal-contractors) , runs GovEagle compliance reviews set up to act like a contracting officer evaluation committee, and saved 30-40% of prep time on RFIs and 15-25% on RFPs.


## Preaward vs. Post-Award Debriefs


Two distinct debrief types exist under the FAR, and which one applies depends on where in the acquisition you were cut.


A preaward debrief, governed by[FAR 15.505](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/15.505) , occurs when your proposal is excluded from the competitive range before award. The agency notifies you of the exclusion, and you have 3 days from that notice to request a debrief in writing. The conversation is narrower, focused on the exclusion decision and not the full source selection.


Post-award debriefs under[FAR 15.506](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/15.506) are more common and more substantive, covering the major weaknesses or deficiencies in your proposal, overall cost or price and technical ratings for you and the awardee, and the rationale for the award decision. Many agencies also walk through strengths and factor-level ratings, but the FAR doesn't require it. Most capture and proposal teams are dealing with this type.


One procedural point worth noting: the FAR allows only one debriefing per proposal. If you're excluded, you can take the debriefing right away or ask to delay it until after award, when it must cover the full post-award content, but a delay doesn't extend your protest deadlines. If you don't request it within 3 days of the exclusion notice, you lose the post-award debriefing as well. Agencies following the FAR Overhaul Part 15 deviation, including DoD since March 2026, cite these rules as FAR 15.206-2 (preaward) and 15.301-1 (post-award).


Preaward Debrief Post-Award Debrief


**FAR Authority** FAR 15.505 (15.206-2 under the FAR Overhaul deviation) FAR 15.506 (15.301-1 under the deviation)


**Trigger** Exclusion from competitive range Not selected for award


**Request Deadline** 3 days after the exclusion notice 3 days after the award notice


**Scope** The agency's evaluation of key elements of your proposal and why it was excluded Major weaknesses or deficiencies, overall cost or price and technical ratings for you and the awardee, and award rationale


**DoD Follow-Up Round** Not applicable Yes (DFARS 215.506-70): 2 business days for written questions, 5 business days for written answers


**Protest Clock Start** 10 days after a timely preaward debriefing is held (a delayed debriefing doesn't extend this) 10 days after the debriefing is held (DoD: after written answers are delivered, if questions were submitted on time)


**How Many** One debriefing per proposal; you may ask to delay it until after award Not available if you were excluded and didn't request a debriefing in time


## Who Can Request a Debrief


Any offeror excluded from the competitive range or not selected for award under a FAR Part 15 negotiated acquisition may request a debrief. That eligibility flows from FAR 15.506 for post-award and FAR 15.505 for preaward, both applying to negotiated procurements structured under[FAR Part 15](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/far-part-15-rfp-guide) .


That right does not carry over automatically to every federal buy. A set-aside run under FAR Part 15 carries the same debriefing rights. Simplified acquisitions and Federal Supply Schedule orders get only a brief explanation on request when the award wasn't based on price alone, and that explanation does not restart the protest clock. Task and delivery orders over $7.5 million under IDIQ contracts get a debriefing under FAR 16.505. Verify the applicable acquisition authority for each specific procurement before assuming entitlement.


## How to Request a Debrief


FAR 15.506 requires a written request submitted within 3 days of receiving the award notice. Count calendar days, but a deadline that lands on a weekend or federal holiday moves to the next business day. Miss that window and your entitlement is gone. Agencies may still honor a late request, but that does not extend your protest deadlines, so treat it as a discretionary exception, not a reliable fallback.


Your request letter should include:


- The solicitation number, so the agency can locate the correct procurement record without back-and-forth.
- A designated point of contact with full contact information, giving the contracting officer a direct line to schedule and confirm the debrief.
- Your preferred format, whether written, oral, or both, so the agency can plan accordingly.


Keep the request professional and direct. Asking for a written debrief, or requesting that an oral session be followed by written responses, gives you a record you can translate into your next proposal effort.


## What the Government Must Disclose


[FAR 15.506(d)](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/15.506) specifies what the agency must cover in a debrief. You are entitled to:


- The major weaknesses or deficiencies the evaluation team found in your proposal
- The overall cost or price (including unit prices) and technical rating for both your firm and the awardee
- The past performance information on your firm
- The overall ranking of all offerors, if the agency developed one
- A summary of the rationale for the award decision
- For commercial products, the make and model the awardee will deliver
- Reasonable answers to relevant questions about whether the source selection followed the solicitation, the FAR, and other applicable rules


What the agency will not share: point-by-point comparisons with other offerors' proposals, trade secrets, other offerors' confidential processes and techniques, confidential commercial and financial information such as cost breakdowns, profit, and indirect cost rates, the names of people who gave past performance references, and anything else exempt under FOIA. The debrief is scoped to your evaluation and the award rationale.


## Enhanced Debriefing Rights for DoD Procurements


Defense contractors operate under a different set of rules for debriefs. Under DFARS 215.506 and 215.506-70 (215.301-70 and 215.301-71 under DoD's FAR Overhaul deviation), DoD procurements carry enhanced post-award debriefing rights that go beyond what the FAR requires.


The core addition is a structured written follow-up round for required post-award debriefings. After the initial debrief, offerors have 2 business days to submit written questions, and the agency must respond in writing within 5 business days of receiving them. The debriefing isn't concluded until those answers are delivered. Congress created this round in the FY2018 NDAA (section 818), and DoD wrote it into the DFARS in 2022. On awards of $15 million or more, the debriefing must be given in writing or orally when requested. Small businesses and nontraditional defense contractors can also request a redacted copy of the source selection decision document on awards over $15 million up to $150 million, and above $150 million the agency must disclose it.


That follow-up window matters because oral debriefs move fast, and processing source selection rationale in real time is difficult. The written Q&A round gives your team a chance to surface what the initial session left open and get documented answers before the protest clock starts.

## Debrief Timelines and the Protest Clock


Timing here is where debrief strategy and protest strategy intersect, and getting the sequence wrong can close off your options entirely.


Under[GAO's bid protest rules](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-4/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-21/section-21.2) , if you requested a required debriefing on time, the 10-day filing window runs from the date the debriefing is held, not from the award notice, and GAO won't accept a protest filed before the offered debriefing date. For DoD procurements under the DFARS enhanced process, if you submit follow-up questions on time, the debriefing doesn't end until the agency delivers its written answers, giving offerors additional runway to assess whether a protest is warranted. A separate deadline matters just as much: to trigger the automatic stay of contract performance, file within 5 days after the offered debriefing date, or 10 days after award if that is later. On DoD awards with timely follow-up questions, those 5 days run from delivery of the written answers.


[GAO's bid protest FAQs](https://www.gao.gov/legal/bid-protests/faqs) say its filing deadlines are strictly enforced and list lateness as grounds for dismissal. In[Hendall Inc.](https://www.gao.gov/products/b-423714.5) (B-423714.5, October 1, 2026), GAO dismissed a protest of a GSA schedule order as late because the agency's later brief explanation of the award did not restart the 10-day clock. Missing the filing window, regardless of how strong the underlying argument is, ends the protest.


If your team is weighing a protest, treat the debrief as part of that decision. Request it promptly, use the written Q&A round on DoD procurements to surface every unanswered question, and track the clock from the correct trigger date. Confusing the award notice with the debriefing date as your protest window start is an unforgiving miscalculation.


## Questions to Ask During a Debrief


Most debrief sessions move quickly, and the questions you bring in determine how much you walk out with.


Structure your questions around the[evaluation factors in Section M](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/section-m-evaluation-factors-for-award) , since that is the scoring framework the panel used. Useful areas to probe:


- Your ratings on each evaluation factor and how they compared to the awardee's overall rating, going beyond a simple pass/fail read
- Specific concerns the evaluators documented about your technical approach or management plan
- How your past performance narrative was received and whether any gaps or relevance issues were noted
- Whether compliance or formatting problems tied to[Section L instructions](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/section-l-instructions-conditions-and-notices-to-bidders) affected scoring before the evaluation panel reached substance
- Which evaluation factors drove the award decision


Keep questions open-ended and aimed at understanding. Phrases like "Can you describe the concern the evaluation team had about..." tend to yield more usable feedback than anything that reads as a challenge to the scoring. The contracting officer usually runs the session and must give reasonable answers to relevant questions about whether the source selection followed the rules, but no one has to re-argue the scores, and evaluators are often more willing to elaborate when the session stays constructive.


On DoD procurements, save your sharpest follow-up questions for the written round. That is your best opportunity to press on anything the oral session left vague, with documented responses you can bring back to your proposal team.


## Common Debrief Mistakes to Avoid


Watch for six mistakes that waste debrief opportunities:


- Missing the 3-day written request deadline, which carries no grace period by right.
- Arriving without prepared questions tied to Section M evaluation factors, since improvised sessions with the[source selection evaluation team](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/sset-source-selection-evaluation-team) tend to produce vague answers; evaluators are more likely to elaborate when questions are specific and structured.
- Treating the debrief as a protest hearing. Adversarial posture shuts down evaluator elaboration quickly.
- Sending only one person. Bring your capture lead, technical lead, and proposal manager so each can process feedback relevant to their lane.
- Taking no written notes or verbatim quotes. Memory degrades; documented evaluator language does not.
- Filing the feedback away without acting on it. A debrief that produces no downstream proposal changes is just a meeting.


## How to Translate Debrief Feedback into Proposal Improvements


Feedback from a debrief is only useful if it enters a workflow. Most teams read the notes once and move on; the ones who[compound win rate](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/benchmark-govcon-win-rate) treat each debrief as structured data.


Start by logging evaluator comments against the specific Section M factor they reference. Over two or three debriefs on similar opportunities, patterns surface: recurring weaknesses in technical approach, past performance relevance gaps, management plan concerns that keep appearing. Those patterns stay invisible if feedback lives in a one-off email thread.


Next, compare what evaluators said against what your team believed were your[win themes](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/win-themes) . Where the panel rated a claimed discriminator as weak or unremarkable, that is a strategy problem, not a writing problem. Flag it for your next capture cycle.


Update your content library with corrected past performance narratives before the next RFP drops. If evaluators flagged a project as too loosely scoped or insufficiently relevant, revise that reference now, while the feedback is specific and fresh. In GovEagle, you can tag past proposals as Won or Lost in the content library and @mention the Won tag in chat, so GovEagle's search draws only on your winning bids.


Finally, feed the debrief back into[bid/no-bid analysis](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/bid-no-bid-decision) for similar follow-on or recompete opportunities. If the gap between your evaluation and the awardee's was structural, that is a[PWin factor](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/pwin-probability-of-win) worth weighing before you commit resources again.

## Final Thoughts on Using the Proposal Debrief Process Strategically


Few things in federal procurement give you this direct a line to what the evaluation panel actually thought. The firms that pull the most from a debrief are the ones who arrive with structured questions, take verbatim notes, and build a workflow that feeds evaluator feedback back into their next proposal. Miss the 3-day deadline or treat the session as a formality, and you give up your best chance at that feedback. Structured debrief follow-through works best when it connects to a traceable proposal workflow, one where every requirement has a planned section and compliance gaps surface in review before the proposal ships, not after a loss. ## FAQ


### How do I use government proposal debrief feedback to fix recurring weaknesses before the next RFP drops?


Log evaluator comments against the specific Section M factor they reference, not as freeform notes. Over two or three debriefs on similar opportunities, patterns in technical approach, past performance relevance, or management plan concerns become visible; those patterns tell you whether you have a strategy problem from capture or a drafting problem at the proposal stage. Revise affected past performance narratives and feed the debrief back into bid/no-bid analysis for follow-on or recompete opportunities before the next solicitation opens.


### What is the difference between a preaward and post-award debrief under FAR 15.505 and FAR 15.506?


A preaward debrief under FAR 15.505 (15.206-2 under the FAR Overhaul deviation) covers the agency's evaluation of key elements of your proposal and why it was excluded from the competitive range. A post-award debrief under FAR 15.506 (15.301-1 under the deviation) covers the major weaknesses or deficiencies in your proposal, overall cost or price and technical ratings for you and the awardee, and the rationale for the award decision. You get one debriefing per proposal: if you're excluded, you can take it right away or ask to delay it until after award, and if you don't request it within 3 days of the exclusion notice, you lose the post-award debriefing too. Most capture and proposal teams are working with post-award debriefs, where the information is more substantive and the protest clock implications are more consequential.


### Should I request a written or oral debrief after losing a DoD contract award?


Request the oral session and ask for written responses to follow-up questions. Under DFARS 215.506-70, required post-award debriefings on DoD awards give you 2 business days after the initial debrief to submit written questions, and the agency must answer in writing within 5 business days. Oral debriefs move fast and processing source selection rationale in real time is difficult, so the written Q&A round is where you surface what the initial session left open and build a documented record. If you submit questions on time, the debriefing isn't concluded, and the GAO filing window doesn't start, until the agency delivers those written answers.


### What's the best way to structure debrief questions around Section M evaluation factors to get useful feedback?


Prepare questions mapped to each Section M evaluation factor before the session instead of improvising, since evaluators are more likely to elaborate when the conversation stays constructive and focused. Ask open-ended questions about specific documented concerns. For example, "Can you describe the concern the evaluation team had about our technical approach on factor two?" yields more usable feedback than anything that reads as challenging the score. Save your sharpest follow-up questions for the written round on DoD procurements, where you get documented answers you can bring directly back to your proposal team.
